newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists, Communists scrap on euro policy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists, Communists scrap on euro policy.

text.p: French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on Wednesday his party would impose its line on a single European currency on its Communist allies if the left won a parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1.
But Communist leader Robert Hue retorted that any attempt to impose one party's hegemony on the left would undermine its credibility and recall the bad old days.

In a France-Inter radio interview, Jospin was asked how he would reconcile differences between the Socialists, who favour European economic and monetary union (EMU) with conditions, and the Communists, who oppose it and want a new referendum.

He said the Communists had evolved positively on Europe, but added: "I told Robert Hue that if there is a majority in which the Socialists have a far bigger contingent than the Communist party...there can only be one line: the one set by the French people which gave the parliamentary majority to the candidates of this party."
The ruling centre-right coalition has warned voters that France could be weakened in Europe if they elect a left-wing coalition with two contradictory positions on monetary union.
But Jospin said: "There won't be both a 'yes' and a 'no' to the single currency. There will be a single line, the one (we) propose to the French people.
"Then it will be up to the Communists to make up their minds freely...They will only be able to participate in government if they are ready to commit themselves to that line," he insisted.

He added that it would be better if the Communists committed themselves for the duration of the five-year legislature rather than dropping out of government in mid-term as they did in the 1984 under Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.

Asked about Jospin's comments, Hue told reporters he did not want to enter into polemics but added: "Any hegemonism by anyone nowadays could give the impression we are going back to what happened in the past.
"That would be very bad and would forfeit much of credibility of the left's efforts to be innovative and modern."
He said the only way France would elect a left-wing majority was if the left united along the lines of the joint declaration the Socialists and Communists signed last week.
That document omitted any direct mention of the single currency but talked of the need to "go beyond the Maastricht treaty on which we did not have the same attitude in the 1992 referendum".

The Socialists' conditions for EMU are the creation of a European "economic government" as a counterweight to the independent central bank, the inclusion of Italy and Spain in the first wave of members, no overvaluation of the euro against the dollar and a pact for growth and solidarity to promote jobs.

Both opposition parties have also said they would reject any further austerity measures to meet the Maastricht criterion of limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for a single currency in 1999.
Jospin said the Communists and Socialists were at least honest in not hiding their differences.
There were deep differences on Europe in the ruling coalition, notably between Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Eurosceptics Charles Pasqua and Philippe Seguin, he charged.

Seguin again denounced the "ultra-liberal logic" of the Maastricht treaty, which he said was hostile to employment, in a speech last week, setting himself apart from the government's orthodox pro-euro policy.
